title: US Escorts 40 Oil Ships Through Hormuz as Transit Nears Pre-War Levels, Putin Signals Diplomatic Path Open on Ukraine
subhead: The Strait of Hormuz is quietly reopening for business under US escort — roughly 18 million barrels moved in a single operation — even as Iran tries to impose a transit fee scheme that Oman has rejected. Separately, Moscow is floating a diplomatic off-ramp on Ukraine, with Ukraine's military intelligence chief revealing an invitation to talks in Moscow.

sections.heading: Hormuz Recovers Under US Escort Even as Iran Pushes a Transit Fee
sections.body:
Oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is approaching its pre-war daily average less than two months after Iran shut the waterway, according to The Black Chronicle. In what news9live and International Business Times described as the biggest US escort operation of the conflict, Washington moved roughly 40 tankers carrying about 18 million barrels in a single escorted convoy through the strait.

The recovery is not uncontested. Business Upturn reports that Oman has publicly rejected Iran's plan to impose a transit fee on shipping through Hormuz, despite the IRGC claiming a deal had been reached — a sign that Tehran's attempt to monetize control of a global chokepoint has not consolidated. Separately, the same outlet notes the US Treasury is warning global banks of severe consequences for facilitating Iran's illicit finances, keeping financial pressure on even as physical transit resumes.
sections.whyItMatters: If Hormuz transit normalizes at pre-war volumes, the most disruptive energy shock of 2026 begins to unwind — a direct check on oil prices and a setback for Iran's bid to convert chokepoint control into permanent leverage.

sections.heading: Putin Opens a Diplomatic Door on Ukraine — and Ukraine's Spy Chief Confirms Moscow Invitation
sections.body:
Moscow is signaling an off-ramp. Putin said the diplomatic path remains open to end the war in Ukraine, as carried by The Chronicle PH, while News18 reported he voiced willingness to restore ties with the US. Kyiv Post, citing military intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov, revealed that Ukraine had been invited to Moscow for talks and a possible meeting with Putin.

The opening is tangled. Hromadske reports the first visit to Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner is in doubt, with Witkoff reported by Kyiv Independent to have gotten cold feet. India's foreign minister S. Jaishankar, fresh off Modi-Putin talks, visited Ukraine this week and backed diplomacy while cautioning that the war cannot be solved by oil purchases alone, per Business Upturn and zoomnews.
sections.whyItMatters: A possible Moscow invitation accepted by Kyiv would mark the first real negotiating channel of the war — but the reported hesitation of Trump's own envoys shows the diplomatic track is fragile before it has truly started.

sections.heading: Germany's Russia Rift Deepens as Leipzig Drone Trail Leads to Serbia and Poland
sections.body:
The investigation into the drone attack on Leipzig airport is broadening beyond Russia. Streamlinefeed reports the probe is tracing a suspect trail that runs through Serbia and Poland, while Airline Routes and Ground Services notes Germany is investigating a possible Serbia link. The suspicion — aired in several outlets including Слободен печат — is that Serbia is being used as a hub for Russian hybrid operations across Europe.

The political fallout is immediate. New Telegraph reports the EU and NATO have vowed to step up pressure on Russia after what they call a new escalation in Germany, and Brand Icon Image notes the Leipzig case is fueling tensions ahead of German elections. Bulgaria's premier, speaking to Anadolu, warned that military efforts to resolve the Ukraine war risk a dangerous escalation — a sign the episode is sharpening the wider Russia-Europe confrontation.
sections.whyItMatters: If European investigators establish a Serbia relay in the Leipzig attack, the incident stops being a lone drone strike and becomes evidence of a Russian hybrid network operating inside the EU's own perimeter — straining EU-Serbia relations and hardening the bloc's Russia posture.

sections.heading: Sudan War Intensifies as UN Finds Foreign Drone Supply Lines
sections.body: A new UN report found that foreign suppliers have boosted the drone capabilities of both sides in Sudan's civil war, and that foreign fighters and weapons are fueling escalating violence, according to Sudans Post and The Eastleigh Voice. The finding lands against a backdrop of renewed movement: Sudan's Burhan inspected Blue Nile troops amid an RSF border buildup, per Streamlinefeed.
sections.whyItMatters: Direct foreign arming of both Sudan's army and the RSF — including drones — internationalizes a conflict that has already displaced millions and threatens to draw in regional powers, with the Horn of Africa's stability hanging on who arms whom next.

sections.heading: Asia Rearms: Taiwan's Defence Budget Crosses NT$1 Trillion
sections.body: Taiwan approved an extra NT$145.7 billion in defence spending, pushing its total budget past NT$1 trillion for the first time, according to defence.newsd.in and News18. The increase comes as The Japan Times argues Taiwan needs a new deterrence strategy, amid continued friction in the South China Sea and rising Chinese military activity in the region.
sections.whyItMatters: Taiwan crossing the trillion-new-taiwan-dollar threshold is a concrete, quantifiable step in the region-wide rearmament underway from Taipei to Tokyo to Seoul — a fiscal signal that deterrence, not reassurance, is the dominant logic of Asia's security dynamics.

bottomLine: Two threads defined September 5: the physical reopening of the world's most important oil chokepoint under US escort — 40 ships and roughly 18 million barrels moved as Hormuz traffic neared pre-war averages, with Oman rejecting Iran's fee scheme — and a tentative diplomatic opening on Ukraine, with Putin declaring the path to peace open and Ukraine's spy chief confirming a Moscow invitation even as Trump's own envoys hesitate. Beneath those headlines, the background conflicts hardened: a UN report documents foreign drone supply lines arming both sides in Sudan, Taiwan's defence budget broke the NT$1 trillion barrier, and Germany's Leipzig drone investigation pulled Serbia and Poland into the trail. The picture is one of a war that may be winding down at its chokepoint while its periphery quietly rearms.
